=== Support Kennedy Burrow.pdf ===
PUC DOCKET NO. 59475
SOAH DOCKET NO. 473-26-16349

APPLICATION OF ONCOR ELECTRIC DELIVERY COMPANY LLC AND LCRA
TRANSMISSION SERVICES CORPORATION TO AMEND THEIR CERTIFICATES
OF CONVENIENCE AND NECESSITY FOR THE BELL COUNTY EAST SWITCH TO
BIG HILL SUBSTATION 765-KV TRANSMISSION LINE PROJECT

CLARE NELSON'S STATEMENT IN SUPPORT OF
ITEM NO. 6571 AND REQUEST FOR INDEPENDENT
VERIFICATION OF ERCOT MODELING
TO THE HONORABLE PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS:

I respectfully submit this statement in support of the request made by Kevin Kennedy and John
Burrow in Item No. 6571, filed September 17, 2026, requesting an independent technical
investigation of the modeling underlying ERCOT's 2024 Permian Basin Reliability Plan
("PBRP"). Item 6571 does not ask the Commission to presume that ERCOT acted improperly.
Rather, it identifies technical questions that warrant independent examination before Texas
proceeds further with transmission projects of this magnitude.

The most important issue raised by Item 6571 is straightforward: Would ERCOT have reached
the same conclusion regarding the need, number, configuration, and capacity of the 765-kV
import paths if the PBRP had been tested using contemporaneous, reconciled system-wide
load and generation assumptions?

Item 6571 identifies apparent differences between the assumptions used in ERCOT's 2024 PBRP
and its contemporaneous 2024 Regional Transmission Plan ("2024 RTP"). The filing
appropriately acknowledges that different planning studies may legitimately use different
assumptions because they address different study years, scenarios, sensitivities, regions, or
planning objectives. The concern is therefore not merely that the two models were different. The
relevant question is whether those differences materially affected ERCOT's system-wide power-
flow results and ultimately its determination that the 765-kV import paths were necessary.

That question should be answered with engineering analysis and data, not assumptions.

Item 6571 explains that changes in the geographic distribution of load and generation can affect
real-power transfers, reactive-power flows, transmission-line loading, interface loading, bus
voltages, generator dispatch, reactive-resource requirements, and the location and severity of
contingency violations. It therefore asks whether the temporal and spatial differences between
the PBRP and 2024 RTP assumptions materially affected the modeled need for the import paths.

I particularly support the proposed counterfactual analysis in Item 6571. It asks an independent
auditor to compare at least three cases: the original PBRP case; a reconciled PBRP case retaining
the intended Permian load forecast while using contemporaneous system-wide assumptions
 elsewhere; and a case using the 2024 RTP's contemporaneous system-wide load and generation
assumptions. The resulting thermal violations, voltage violations, transfer capability, limiting
elements, contingency severity, required import capacity, number of import paths, voltage level,
and required facilities could then be compared.

That analysis could provide an empirical answer to the central question rather than requiring the
Commission, landowners, or ratepayers to speculate.

Item 6571 also raises an important question concerning the relationship between the PBRP and
subsequent 2024 RTP modeling. According to the filing, the subsequent RTP analysis
incorporated the three PBRP 765-kV import paths into its starting case. The Commission should
therefore determine whether subsequent modeling independently validated the original need for
those facilities or instead assumed those facilities as part of the starting system.

I am not asking the Commission to conclude from Item 6571 that ERCOT's modeling was
incorrect, that ERCOT violated a NERC Reliability Standard, or that the 765-kV import paths
are unnecessary. Those are precisely the questions that independent verification should
answer.

The stakes justify that verification. The PBRP's three 765-kV import paths total approximately
1,255 miles of new bulk transmission, according to Item 6571. The Commission's decisions
concerning these projects affect Texas electric customers, communities, and landowners whose
property may be subject to condemnation for transmission rights-of-way.

The Commission should therefore require ERCOT to make available to an appropriately
qualified independent reviewer the underlying modeling information necessary to reproduce and
test the PBRP conclusions, subject to appropriate protections for confidential or security-
sensitive information.

At a minimum, the independent review should determine:

   1. Whether the PBRP's system-wide load, generation, topology, and forecast assumptions
      were appropriate for determining the need for the 765-kV import paths;
   2. Why materially different assumptions appear in the contemporaneous PBRP and 2024
      RTP models and whether those differences were technically appropriate for their
      respective purposes;
   3. Whether reconciling the PBRP with contemporaneous system-wide load and generation
      assumptions materially changes the identified reliability violations, transfer requirements,
      or need for any of the three 765-kV import paths;
   4. Whether each import path was independently demonstrated to be necessary;
   5. What steady-state, dynamic, contingency, and transfer-capability analyses actually
      established the need and required capacity of each import path; and
   6. Whether subsequent ERCOT studies independently confirmed the need for the PBRP
      import paths or incorporated those facilities into the starting topology without
      independently re-establishing their need.
 These questions are consistent with the detailed audit methodology proposed in Item 6571,
including its request for reconciliation of bus-level load and generation assumptions,
identification of forecast vintages, reconstruction of model genealogy, counterfactual analysis,
and an independent determination of whether each 765-kV path remains necessary under a
reconciled model.

These questions are also relevant to the Commission's current remand.

The remand requires further consideration of issues bearing on the need for the proposed Bell
County East to Big Hill project. To the extent Issues 11 and 13 require findings concerning the
need for this project and the adequacy of the evidence supporting that need, the reliability of the
underlying ERCOT modeling is not a collateral matter. It goes directly to the foundation upon
which the asserted need for this 765-kV facility rests. A remand intended to resolve unanswered
questions concerning need should not simply assume the validity of the underlying modeling if
substantial, technically testable questions concerning that modeling have now been placed before
the Commission. Independent verification would provide a stronger evidentiary basis for
resolving those issues rather than prejudging their outcome.

Independent verification should not be viewed as an attack on ERCOT. If the PBRP assumptions
and methodology are technically sound and the 765-kV import paths remain necessary when
tested against reconciled system-wide assumptions, an independent analysis should demonstrate
that. If the results materially change, the Commission should know that before relying upon
those results to authorize additional facilities.

For these reasons, I respectfully request that the Commission give serious consideration to Item
No. 6571 and order an independent technical review sufficient to answer these questions
before relying further on the disputed PBRP modeling as the basis for determining the
need for the Bell County East to Big Hill 765-kV project and related PBRP 765-kV import
facilities.

Respectfully submitted,

Clare Nelson
Affected Landowner
PUC Docket No. 59475
